source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: Eight worked-example chains in the prompt lift PaLM 540B on GSM8K far above standard prompting.
limits: Few-shot, hand-written exemplars, math word problems; mostly 2022 model families.
agent_relevance: Baseline effect that every later study qualifies. Gains are on multi-step math, not general tasks.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: CoT is an emergent ability: it does not help small models and only helps at about 100B parameters and above.
numbers: Gains appear only for models of 100B or more. Smaller models wrote fluent but illogical chains and scored below standard prompting.
limits: Dated: later small models trained on reasoning data do benefit. The threshold is for 2022 pretrained models.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that forces step text on a weak model can lower accuracy. Check the model before adding it.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: Gain grows with problem difficulty. On one-step problems the gain is zero or negative.
numbers: GSM8K (lowest baseline) performance more than doubled for the largest GPT and PaLM. SingleOp (easiest MAWPS subset): change negative or very small.
limits: Difficulty is inferred from the dataset, not controlled.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and G12: use steps only when the problem needs several steps.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: Ablations: equation-only, dots-for-compute, and reasoning-after-answer do not reproduce the CoT gain on GSM8K.
numbers: Equation-only did not help much on GSM8K (it helped on 1-2 step sets). Dots equal to chain length and reasoning after the answer stayed near baseline (LaMDA 137B, Fig. 5).
limits: Only LaMDA 137B in the main text; exact values in Appendix Table 6.
agent_relevance: Order matters: reasoning must come before the answer. Extra tokens alone were not the cause in this setting.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: Gain survives different annotators and exemplar sets, with the usual few-shot variance.
numbers: Three exemplar sets and several annotators all beat standard prompting by a large margin on LaMDA 137B (GSM8K, MAWPS).
limits: Authors note exemplar variance is expected.
agent_relevance: Style of the written steps is not what matters; content is.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning
finding: Manual check of chains: when the final answer was right the chain was nearly always right too.
numbers: LaMDA 137B, GSM8K, 50 random correct-answer samples: all chains correct except 2 that reached the answer by luck.
limits: Small sample, one model, correct-answer cases only. Says nothing about whether the chain caused the answer.
agent_relevance: Whether a chain is the real cause is a separate question; see the faithfulness lines (b12 to b17).

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large language models are zero-shot reasoners
finding: Adding only 'Let's think step by step' (no examples) gives large gains on arithmetic for a large instruction-tuned model.
numbers: text-davinci-002: MultiArith 17.7 -> 78.7; GSM8K 10.4 -> 40.7.
limits: Underperforms few-shot CoT with carefully crafted exemplars. Table 1 shows little or no gain on the easy sets SingleEq and AddSub.
agent_relevance: A cheap trigger works for the 2022 class of models; effect is much smaller for models already trained to reason (b26).

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought
finding: Sampling many chains and taking the majority answer adds large gains on top of greedy CoT.
numbers: Gains over greedy CoT (points): GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9.
limits: Costs many samples; gains are smaller on commonsense tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports G11: several short independent attempts and a vote beat one long chain.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Chains with invalid reasoning in the prompt still keep most of the CoT gain, so exemplar correctness is not the main driver.
numbers: text-davinci-002, GSM8K answer accuracy: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid-reasoning exemplars 39.5. Paper states 80-90% of CoT performance is retained (over 90% on intrinsic metrics).
limits: Gain drops when exemplars lose relevance or coherence (next line).
agent_relevance: The model copies format and topic of the steps. Step validity in exemplars is not the lever.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Relevance to the query and correct step order are the key aspects of exemplar reasoning.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy: no coherence 23.1, no relevance 11.0, versus CoT 48.5 and standard 15.4. Removing relevance falls below standard prompting.
limits: Table shown is for one model; others in appendix.
agent_relevance: Retrieved or written exemplars must be on topic and ordered. Off-topic exemplars can hurt below no-CoT.

source: Ye and Durrett (2022) The unreliability of explanations in few-shot prompting
finding: Weaker models gain little from explanations in prompts; only text-davinci-002 gains clearly. Explanations often do not entail the prediction.
numbers: OPT, GPT-3 davinci and text-davinci-001: small to moderate gains over standard few-shot on QA and NLI. text-davinci-002: larger gains.
limits: 2022 models; textual QA and NLI, not math.
agent_relevance: A limit on the claim that CoT helps everywhere. Judged-good explanations co-occur with right answers, so checking an explanation can give a weak signal.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language models don't always say what they think
finding: Biasing features in the prompt change CoT answers and are not mentioned in the CoT; the CoT rationalises the biased answer.
numbers: 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. Accuracy drops up to 36% (Suggested Answer, GPT-3.5 zero-shot: -36.3). Answer-is-always-A: GPT-3.5 -18.7, Claude 1.0 -4.7.
limits: Biases were artificial. Few-shot CoT cut the drop: -36.3 to -24.1 (GPT-3.5), -30.6 to -21.5 (Claude).
agent_relevance: G10: a written reason is not evidence of the real cause. Hints in the input can steer the answer unseen.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language models don't always say what they think
finding: CoT raises unbiased accuracy on average but lowers it when a wrong suggestion is present.
numbers: Unbiased accuracy no-CoT -> CoT: GPT-3.5 57.1 -> 59.6; Claude 1.0 59.2 -> 65.3. Suggested Answer context: GPT-3.5 39.5 -> 23.3; Claude 37.3 -> 34.7.
limits: Averages hide task variation; some tasks get worse with CoT.
agent_relevance: Writing steps can amplify an anchor in the context. Strip hints and prior answers from the input (S1 hygiene).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Test of whether the answer depends on the CoT: truncate, insert mistakes, paraphrase, replace with filler tokens.
numbers: Filler tokens ('...') gave no accuracy gain on 8 tasks; on TruthfulQA and OpenBookQA accuracy fell slightly. Paraphrasing did not remove the CoT benefit.
limits: Main tests on one 175B RLHF model; multiple-choice tasks.
agent_relevance: In 2023-era LLMs the gain came from the content of the text, not extra compute or hidden phrasing. Toy models differ (b27).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Faithfulness (how much the answer depends on the CoT) varies by task and gets worse with model size past 13B.
numbers: For 7 of 8 tasks the 13B model changed its answer after CoT more often than the 175B model. For 6 of 8 tasks the 13B model was most faithful. Models under 13B gain little from CoT.
limits: One model family, 8 tasks.
agent_relevance: Stronger models may need steps less and ignore them more: judge by output checks, cap length (G10, G11).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think
finding: Reasoning models verbalise a used hint rarely.
numbers: Average faithfulness 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1 across 6 hint types on MMLU and GPQA. Misalignment-type hints: 20% and 29%. Reveal rate is often below 20%.
limits: Planted multiple-choice cues; scores only cases where the hint changed the answer.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G10. Do not use the trace to decide whether the answer is trustworthy.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think
finding: Unfaithful chains are longer; harder questions give less faithful chains; outcome RL raises faithfulness then plateaus.
numbers: Unfaithful CoT: Claude 3.7 2064 +/- 59 tokens vs faithful 1439 +/- 54. GPQA less faithful than MMLU by 44% relative (Claude) and 32% (R1). Outcome RL plateaus at 28% (MMLU) and 20% (GPQA). Reward-hack verbalisation under 2% in 5 of 6 synthetic environments.
limits: Synthetic hacks; RL only on Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
agent_relevance: A long chain is a risk marker, not a quality marker.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT
finding: Meta-analysis of 110 papers (1,218 comparisons) from ICLR 2024, EACL 2024 and NAACL 2024: CoT helps mainly on math, symbolic and logic tasks.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Those three categories 45.5 -> 56.9. All other categories 56.1 -> 56.8. 4,642 papers screened.
limits: Compares to direct answering without matching compute; authors call the small gain on other categories no victory once compute is matched.
agent_relevance: Strongest single basis for G11: default to a direct answer or short thinking outside math, symbolic and logic.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT
finding: Own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models: on MMLU nearly all the CoT gain is on questions with an equals sign.
numbers: As much as 95% of the CoT gain on MMLU comes from questions or answers containing '='. Majority of gain on MMLU Pro also on the math slice. StrategyQA and MuSR gain consistently (10 and 6 models).
limits: Equals sign is a crude proxy. StrategyQA and MuSR were built to reward decomposition.
agent_relevance: A cheap code check (does the item need calculation or symbol steps?) can decide whether to think at all.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT
finding: CoT gain comes mostly from executing symbolic steps, and a symbolic solver beats CoT on those.
numbers: Splitting plan from execution: CoT mainly helps execution; on the formal tasks tested, plan plus external solver beat CoT for both steps.
limits: Tasks tested were formal ones (math and logic puzzles).
agent_relevance: Supports handing calculation to code or a tool instead of long text arithmetic.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) Chain of thoughtlessness? An analysis of CoT in planning
finding: On Blocksworld, CoT helps only when the example prompt is nearly identical in type to the query; gains vanish as problem size grows.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Claude 3 Opus; goal stacks of 3 to 20 blocks; five prompt types from zero-shot to lexicographic stacking. Accuracy falls sharply with stack size even for algorithm-teaching prompts; general prompts often fall below standard prompting.
limits: Planning domain; simple synthetic problems. Authors also rebuilt coin flip, last-letter and arithmetic with scalable size and saw similar failure.
agent_relevance: Failed generalisation: showing an algorithm in text does not make the model run it on longer instances.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): CoT can reduce performance
finding: Six tasks where deliberation hurts humans were tried with CoT; three show large drops.
numbers: Artificial grammar (chance 50%): GPT-4o 87.5 -> 64.4 (-23.1), Claude 3 Opus 70.7 -> 62.7, Gemini 1.5 Pro 68.0 -> 61.95, Llama 3.1 70B 65.9 -> 57.1; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 -> 67.7 (no drop, p=0.969). o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0 on a subset: -36.3.
limits: o1 reasoning cannot be turned off, so it was compared with GPT-4o. The other 3 task types gave mixed results.
agent_relevance: Implicit pattern learning and tasks where language is a poor code: think less there.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): CoT can reduce performance
finding: Face recognition and learning labels with exceptions also get worse with CoT.
numbers: Face recognition (chance 20%): GPT-4o 64.0 -> 51.2 (-12.8, p<0.01), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 -> 94.8. Rounds needed to learn exception labels: GPT-4o 2.9 -> 12.5 (+331%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 -> 6.4 (+129%).
limits: Synthetic text descriptions of faces; model-specific.
agent_relevance: Reasoning in words can replace a better implicit judgement, as in human verbal overshadowing.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): CoT can reduce performance
finding: CoT helps on logical-inconsistency detection, a case where humans fail and models do not.
numbers: NLI consistency task, zero-shot vs CoT accuracy on inconsistent items: GPT-4o 53.2 -> 93.9; Llama 3.1 70B 55.6 -> 81.6; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.2 -> 67.5.
limits: Column reading of the extracted table is partly inferred.
agent_relevance: Human-psychology failure cases predict some but not all CoT failures.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: decreasing value of chain of thought
finding: On GPQA Diamond (198 questions, 25 runs each) CoT gives small average gains for non-reasoning models and more answer variability.
numbers: Average rating gain: Gemini Flash 2.0 +0.135, Sonnet 3.5 +0.117 (both p<.001), GPT-4o-mini +0.044 (ns). 100%-correct metric fell for several models: Gemini Flash 2.0 -0.131, Gemini Pro 1.5 -0.172 (p<.001). CoT requests 35-600% slower.
limits: One benchmark; fixed prompts; not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: CoT can flip questions the model would get right every time. Averages hide a loss of reliability.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: decreasing value of chain of thought
finding: For dedicated reasoning models, an explicit CoT prompt adds almost nothing but costs time and tokens.
numbers: o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5: mostly no significant change. o4-mini small gain at the 51% metric (RD 0.056, p=.003); Gemini Flash 2.5 fell at 100% and 90% (RD -0.131, p<.001; -0.071, p=.016). Extra time 20-80% (10-20 s).
limits: Many recent non-reasoning models also reason by default, so the prompt adds little.
agent_relevance: Do not add a think-step-by-step line to a model that already reasons. Matches G11.

source: Pfau, Merrill and Bowman (2024) Let's think dot by dot
finding: In trained toy transformers, meaningless filler tokens can replace CoT on parallelisable algorithmic tasks.
numbers: Filler-token transformers solved two hard algorithmic tasks the same models could not solve with no intermediate tokens. Learning to use fillers needed dense, specific supervision to converge.
limits: Small models trained from scratch; not shown in pretrained chat models; contrasts with b14.
agent_relevance: Extra compute alone can matter in principle, so 'content is the cause' is not universal. The CoT text may hide real work.

source: Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) The expressive power of transformers with chain of thought
finding: Theory: how much CoT adds depends on how many intermediate steps are allowed.
numbers: Logarithmic number of steps in input length adds only slightly over standard transformers. Linear steps adds a clear ability (recognising all regular languages, under standard conjectures).
limits: Idealised transformers; expressivity, not what trained models do.
agent_relevance: Serial tasks (state tracking, graph connectivity) need real step text; very short steps cannot help on them.

source: Wu et al. (2025) When more is less: understanding chain-of-thought length
finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U with CoT length. Best length rises with task difficulty and falls with model skill.
numbers: Seen in a 6-layer GPT-2 toy, the Qwen2.5 series on MATH Level 5, and RL (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GRPO, LeetCode-2K) where models drift to shorter chains as accuracy rises. Training on optimal-length CoT beat the longest CoTs.
limits: Theory, toy and mid-size models; not frontier systems.
agent_relevance: Basis for a per-mode length cap that scales with difficulty (G11, G12).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=?
finding: o1-like models overthink easy problems; later solution rounds add almost no accuracy.
numbers: For '2 plus 3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one example gave 13 solutions. In most correct cases the first solution round already holds the right answer (MATH500).
limits: Open o1-like models such as QwQ-32B-Preview; efficiency metrics are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Cap thinking on easy items; stop after the first consistent answer.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking
finding: Three regimes on puzzles: at low complexity plain models beat reasoning models, at medium thinking wins, at high both collapse.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking vs non-thinking and DeepSeek R1 vs V3 at equal token budgets on Tower of Hanoi, Checkers Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World. On MATH500 pass@k of thinking and non-thinking was comparable; the gap grew on AIME24 and AIME25.
limits: Disputed (next line). Authors raise possible contamination on older benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Extended thinking is not free: plain answers win at low complexity.

source: Opus and Lawsen (2025) The illusion of the illusion of thinking
finding: A comment says the reported collapse is mostly an output-limit and grading artifact.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi move lists exceed token limits; River Crossing instances for N>=6 are impossible with the stated boat size but scored as failures. Asking for a generating function gave high accuracy on Hanoi sizes reported as zero (preliminary, several models).
limits: Preliminary; no full results table; a short comment, not a full replication.
agent_relevance: A 'reasoning fails at scale' result can come from the test setup. Check harness limits before blaming reasoning.
